![](assets/profile.jpg){fig-alt="Shokhrukhkhon Nishonkulov" width="320"}

My name is **Shokhrukhkhon Nishonkulov**, and I am currently pursuing a Master of Science in Economics at the University of Bonn. Economics, for me, is not just a field of study it is a way of thinking. It shapes how I approach problems, how I structure ideas, and how I try to understand the world.

I began my academic journey at Kokand University in Uzbekistan, where I completed my undergraduate degree in Economics. During those years, I discovered a deep interest in quantitative analysis and research. What started as curiosity about models and data gradually turned into a commitment to rigorous, structured thinking. I learned that good research is not about complexity for its own sake, but about clarity, asking precise questions and answering them carefully.

At Bonn, my work focuses on econometrics, especially high-dimensional methods and causal inference. I am currently studying the finite-sample behavior of the Double LASSO estimator through extensive Monte Carlo simulations. I am interested not only in whether a method works in theory, but how it performs in practice, where data are imperfect, assumptions are stretched, and real decisions depend on reliable inference.

My broader interests include applied econometrics, institutional economics, public finance, and the design of research tools that make complex methods transparent and reproducible.

Outside formal research, I enjoy building things whether it is a research workflow, a website, a startup idea, or a collaborative project. I have been fortunate to lead and participate in international startup competitions, experiences that taught me resilience, teamwork, and the value of disciplined execution.

Outside academia, I have led and participated in international startup competitions, building projects from scratch with small teams under tight constraints. Those experiences taught me something classrooms cannot fully teach — how to move from idea to execution, how to make decisions under uncertainty, and how to stay persistent when things do not work the first time.

At the core of everything I do is a simple principle: think clearly, work seriously, and always aim to connect theory with real-world problems. I am motivated by complex problems, but I believe the way to approach them is simple: think carefully, test honestly, and build patiently.
